article.overview: A radiation spectrometer is an instrument that measures how much energy ionising radiation carries and how that energy is distributed, by detecting individual particles or photons and sorting them by the energy they deposit in a sensitive detector. For the Moon, such instruments help characterise the cosmic-ray and solar-particle environment that crews, electronics and hardware must withstand [2][3]. This article uses two Moon-related examples: the Cosmic Ray Telescope for the Effects of Radiation (CRaTER) on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), and the Radiation Dose Monitor (RADOM) flown on India's Chandrayaan-1 mission [4][5][6]. Both were flown. The two instruments differ greatly in scale and measurement approach, so their values are not directly comparable.
article.description: A typical radiation spectrometer uses one or more solid-state detectors, often silicon, arranged so that a particle passing through several layers can be identified. Each layer records the energy deposited in it, and electronics combine these signals to estimate the particle's energy and type. CRaTER follows this pattern: it is a stack of silicon detector pairs separated by tissue-equivalent plastic, so that the energy deposited behind a known thickness of material can be measured [3]. RADOM uses a single silicon detector and records the deposited-energy spectrum in 256 channels [6]. The general stacking principle described here is background knowledge and is not drawn from the cited sources.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The stated purpose of CRaTER is to characterise the deep-space radiation environment by measuring linear energy transfer (LET) spectra of galactic and solar cosmic rays, particularly at energies above 10 MeV, and to test radiation-effects and shielding models by comparing predicted and measured LET spectra [3]. LET describes how much energy a charged particle deposits per unit distance as it travels through matter, so an LET spectrum shows how often particles of each deposition level arrive. NASA describes the instrument as characterising the lunar radiation environment and determining its potential biological impacts [2]. For RADOM, the ISSDC payload document lists the objectives as measuring particle flux, the deposited-energy spectrum and accumulated dose rates in lunar orbit, and studying radiation hazards to support evaluation of shielding requirements for future crewed lunar missions [5]. The RADOM paper describes the instrument as monitoring the local radiation environment in near-Earth space and in lunar space [6].
article.operating_principle: When a charged particle passes through a silicon detector, it deposits an amount of energy that depends on its charge, its speed and the thickness of material it crosses. The CRaTER team describes thin and thick detector pairs: each thin detector feeds a low-gain amplifier and each thick detector a high-gain amplifier, so that together they cover the full LET range expected [3]. Comparing signals across the detectors helps identify the path of an individual particle [3]. The general physics in this paragraph is background and is not drawn from the cited sources. RADOM's absorbed dose is calculated from its recorded spectrum: a calibrated sum over the 256 channel counts, divided by the mass of the sensitive part of the detector [6].
article.scientific_importance: The Moon has no thick atmosphere to slow incoming particles, so its surface and nearby orbit are exposed to galactic and solar radiation [general background, not drawn from the cited sources]. NASA states that LRO has measured the lunar radiation environment in unprecedented detail [1]. Measured LET spectra are useful because they can be compared with radiation-effects and shielding models, which are needed to design protection for crews and electronics [3]. RADOM recorded the Earth's radiation belts, galactic cosmic rays and a solar energetic particle event during the Chandrayaan-1 mission, and its authors describe its performance as nominal in comparison with similar instruments on the International Space Station [6]. Its low-energy thresholds for electrons and protons limit which particle populations it can detect [6].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a radiation spectrometer. Requirements depend on the particle energy range to be measured, the required geometry, whether the instrument sits on an orbiter or a surface platform, and the available mass, power and data resources. The two examples are not interchangeable, and their values are not directly compared. Where a value is not publicly specified in the accessed sources, it is stated as such and not estimated.

examples.name: Cosmic Ray Telescope for the Effects of Radiation (CRaTER), Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
examples.launch_context: LRO launched on June 18, 2009 [1]. Current operational status and post-2009 data history not verified in the accessed sources.
examples.sensor_configuration: Aluminium end caps shield the detectors from low-energy particles, followed by three thin-and-thick silicon detector pairs (six detectors) surrounding two sections of A-150 tissue-equivalent plastic [3].
examples.telescope_dimensions: Not separately stated in the accessed source.
examples.let_resolution: Below 0.3% of maximum LET in each range (net RSS value including detector and electronics noise, and gain uncertainty).
examples.qualification: Values are from the paper's summary table for the as-delivered flight unit [3]. The paper describes them as optimal values from trade studies, so they should be read as flight-unit values from a 2010 publication.

examples.name: Radiation Dose Monitor (RADOM), Chandrayaan-1
examples.launch_context: Chandrayaan-1 launched on 22 October 2008 [4]. RADOM was the first experiment switched on after launch and was operational until the end of the mission [6]. ISRO states that communication was lost on 29 August 2009 [4].
examples.sensor_configuration: Single silicon PIN detector, 0.3 mm thick, 2 cm2 area; one charge-sensitive preamplifier (Amptek A225F); 12-bit ADC; two microcontrollers and buffer memory [5][6].
examples.exposure_time_note: The arXiv paper describes a typical 30 s exposure that can be changed by ground command [6]; the ISSDC document states it is fixed at 30 s [5].
examples.mass_reported_values: Approximately 100 g [6]; 160 g for the instrument [5]. Unresolved.
examples.power_note: Not stated in the accessed sources [5][6].
examples.qualification: The arXiv paper reports flight results and describes the flight model [6]. The ISSDC document gives pre-launch objectives and configuration [5]. The channel-to-energy calibration is not stated in the accessed sources.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The two examples differ in scale and design. CRaTER is a telescope on an orbiter, with a 5.53 kg flight unit and an electronics box of about 24 cm by 23 cm by 16 cm [3]. RADOM is a small single-detector unit of about 10 by 5 by 2 cm [6]. No proportions are estimated beyond these published figures.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The CRaTER flight-unit mass is 5.53 kg [3]. The RADOM mass is reported as about 100 g [6] in one source and 160 g [5] in another, so it is recorded as unresolved. The LRO spacecraft mass is a spacecraft figure and is not an instrument mass.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: CRaTER's flight-unit power is 6.66 W [3]. RADOM's power requirement is not stated in the accessed sources, so no value is given.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: CRaTER operates in lunar polar orbit as part of LRO [3]. Its electronics box and telescope assembly are electrically isolated from each other, and the telescope is grounded through its signal path to reduce noise on the spacecraft chassis [3]. The accessed sources do not state thermal, vacuum, radiation-tolerance or operating-temperature limits for CRaTER. For RADOM, the accessed sources do not state environmental limits. As general background, a radiation instrument must survive the same space environment it measures, including thermal cycling and radiation damage to its electronics; this is not drawn from the cited sources.
article.limitations: The main limitation is that the two examples are separate instruments on different missions, with different designs and purposes, and they cannot be used to infer a common specification. The CRaTER values come from a 2010 paper describing the as-delivered flight unit [3]. The RADOM mass is inconsistent between sources, and its power is not stated [5][6]. A radiation spectrometer measures a particle environment, so its results depend on orbit, solar activity and the shielding in front of the detector, not only on the instrument.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: CRaTER was carried on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, so its relevant interfaces are those of an orbiting spacecraft rather than a lander. RADOM was part of the Chandrayaan-1 payload; its mounting and integration arrangements are not described in the accessed sources.
transportation_process: Earth integration: for CRaTER, the electronics box bolts to the spacecraft through six feet along its base, and four spacecraft connectors relay commands and telemetry, provide power and supply a timing signal [3]. RADOM's integration is not described in the accessed sources.
Launch: LRO launched on June 18, 2009 [1]; the launch vehicle is not stated in the accessed NASA page. Chandrayaan-1 launched on October 22, 2008 [4].

Lunar transfer and orbit insertion: general background for lunar orbiter missions; not verified for either instrument. RADOM's measurements during transfer and lunar-orbit capture are reported in [6].
Commissioning and operations: RADOM was switched on soon after launch [6]. CRaTER's commissioning sequence is not verified in the accessed sources.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Neither example involves surface deployment in the accessed sources. CRaTER is an orbiter instrument [2][3], and RADOM is described as an instrument on Chandrayaan-1 [6]. No deployment mechanism, surface setup or lander cabling is claimed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: CRaTER is one of LRO's seven science instruments [2]. RADOM was one of Chandrayaan-1's scientific payloads [4][5], and it recorded data from the Earth-to-Moon transfer and from lunar orbit [6].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander or rover compatibility is assessed or claimed for either example. The accessed sources do not provide interface evidence for a lunar lander, rover or surface installation. A future radiation spectrometer would need its own mass, power, thermal and data-interface definition.

article.historical_significance: LRO's radiation instrument is part of the record of NASA's post-Apollo lunar exploration. NASA states that LRO measured the lunar radiation environment in unprecedented detail [1]. CRaTER was designed to test radiation-effects and shielding models using measured LET spectra [3]. RADOM's observations on Chandrayaan-1 were presented as a record of radiation belts, galactic cosmic rays and a solar energetic particle event in the Earth-Moon environment [6].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: This article is limited by the sources accessed in this run. The CRaTER data-product and operational history after 2009 are not verified. The CRaTER paper was read as a copy hosted by a research team [3]; the journal record was not separately accessed. For RADOM, the mass is inconsistent between sources [5][6], power is not stated, and the exposure time is described as typically 30 s, changeable by ground command, in one source [6] and as fixed in another [5]. The RADOM paper also contains dose values with inconsistent units, so only flux and dose-rate values stated with their orbit context are quoted here. The ISRO page's specification table gives the orbit as 100 km by 100 km [4], whereas the RADOM paper describes a 100 km orbit followed by a 200 km orbit [6]. The ISRO and ISSDC documents do not name an institution for every payload, although the ISSDC document names the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences as the origin of RADOM [5]. No image was verified as a direct, rights-cleared asset, so the article has no images. General physics and lunar-environment background is labelled as not drawn from the cited sources.

data_quality_notes: RADOM mass conflict: approximately 100 g in the arXiv paper [6] versus 160 g for the instrument in the ISSDC document [5]. Detector mass 139.8 mg is from [5]. Unresolved; mass_kg is null.
RADOM power is not stated in either accessed source [5][6]; power_w is null.
RADOM exposure time: typically 30 s and changeable by ground command in [6]; fixed at 30 s in [5].

The RADOM arXiv paper contains dose values with inconsistent units (for example, microgray per hour versus gray per hour, and a cumulative transfer dose stated in gray). Only flux and dose-rate values stated with their orbit context are summarised; the cumulative figure is not quoted.
Orbit description differs: the ISRO specification table gives 100 km x 100 km [4]; the arXiv paper describes 100 km and then 200 km [6].

CRaTER values are from the 2010 Space Science Reviews paper's summary table for the as-delivered flight unit [3], read from an accessed copy. The DOI record and any later CRaTER specifications were not separately accessed.
A search snippet suggested that CRaTER's endcaps block protons below about 13 MeV. This was not found in the accessed paper text and is not included.
